original_question: Let V be a variety generated by a finite group, and let f(n)p be the order of the free group in V on n generators. Is it true that the sequence n log f(n) has a limit as n → ∞, and this limit is an integer?
target_in_paper: Open Problem 21.102 in the section "New Problems (21st issue, 2026)". Its official wording asks whether, for a variety V generated by a finite group and f(n) equal to the order of the free group in V on n generators, the sequence (log f(n))^(1/n) has a limit as n -> infinity, and whether that limit is an integer.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the relevant problem as one about a group variety generated by a finite group, uses f(n) for the order of the n-generated free object in that variety, and asks for both existence of an asymptotic limit and integrality of that limit.
missing_details: The main asymptotic expression is the n-th root of log f(n), i.e. (log f(n))^(1/n), not the product n log f(n). This is the key paper-faithful correction.
To make the question stand-alone, the phrase "the free group in V on n generators" should be stated as the relatively free group of rank n in the variety V.
The index set should be explicit: n ranges over positive integers.
The paper leaves "log" unspecified; a stand-alone formulation should fix a base, for example the natural logarithm.
It is clearer to name the relatively free group, e.g. F_V(n), and then define f(n) = |F_V(n)|.
refined_question: Let V be a variety of groups generated by a finite group. For each integer n >= 1, let F_V(n) denote the relatively free group of rank n in V, and set f(n) = |F_V(n)|. Is it true that the limit lim_{n->infinity} (log f(n))^(1/n) exists, and that this limit is always an integer?
justification: The draft is targeting Problem 21.102 almost verbatim. The scope is already correct, but the crucial asymptotic quantity has been garbled: the official problem concerns the n-th root of log f(n), not n log f(n). Since this arXiv item is a problem collection rather than a standard theorem-paper, the sharpest paper-faithful refinement is simply the official notebook problem rewritten with the relatively free group notation made explicit.
